title: Canary change scratchpad — small refactor canaries
content:
Purpose: quick, messy personal notes for running tiny refactor canaries safely. This is my scratchpad for the next few small-rollouts (kv-cache key normalization, header parsing refactor). Not a finished playbook — rough steps, heuristics, and things to validate before I hit canary route.

Top-level goals:
- Deploy very small changes behind a canary toggle (route-level split) with easy rollback.
- Exercise the change against real traffic sample (1%-5%) with automated smoke checks.
- Capture metrics that matter to inference: p50/p95 latency, token throughput, kv-cache hit rate, mem pressure, error rate, and client API error/timeout rates.
- Fail fast and auto-fallback if any SLO/DB/Cache regressions.

Quick checklist before canary:
- [ ] PR has unit tests + a couple of sticky integration tests (local runtime + small model).
- [ ] Add feature flag gate (route param or env toggle) with default OFF.
- [ ] Add explicit telemetry events: "canary.started","canary.hit","canary.fallback","canary.rolled_back"
- [ ] Add debug counters for the exact code path (so we can tell how many requests used new path).
- [ ] Smoke tests written (see smoke commands below).
- [ ] Add a small sample loadbench (100 concurrent, seq len 128, model small) we can run in staging.
- [ ] Approve rollback path in config (fast switch to main model/route).

Routing plan (proposal):
- Create a canary route: /v1/llm/generate?canary=kv2 (or HTTP header X-Canary: kv2).
- Use smart routing to send 1% of production traffic for first 30m, then 5% for 2 hours if stable.
- If backend latency or errors exceed thresholds -> 100% fallback to previous route.

Metric thresholds (initial conservative values):
- p95 latency increase > +30% absolute OR p50 > +50ms -> abort.
- error rate (5xx or client timeouts) > 0.5% absolute above baseline -> abort.
- kv-cache hit rate drop > 10% absolute -> abort.
- mem usage increase > 500MB per instance -> abort.
- any observed model correctness regression on sampled prompts -> manual pause.

Smoke commands (manual verification):
- quick curl against canary route (local/staging):
  curl -s -X POST https://staging.redwood.ai/v1/llm/generate \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer $STAGING_KEY' \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -H 'X-Canary: kv2' \
    -d '{"model":"small-test","input":"Summarize: The quick brown fox"}' | jq '.'
- tail logs for canary tag: 
  k logs -l app=redwood-api --since=10m | rg 'canary.*kv2'
- verify telemetry event appears in tracing/otel and traces show the path name.

Test harness ideas to simulate real load:
- Traffic sampler: replay real production requests (sanitized) to canary route for 15m. Use differences in sequence lengths and batch sizes.
- Use the small-loadbench in /scripts/loadbench/canary-sim.py (TODO: write) to generate mix of chat/generate/embeddings to measure end-to-end.
- Run a short growth test: 100rps for 10m, 500rps for 2m spike, monitor tail latencies.

Instrumentation to add in PR (small patches):
- Counters: canary_kv2_requests, canary_kv2_path_fallbacks, canary_kv2_kv_hit, canary_kv2_kv_miss.
- Tag traces with canary.name=kv2, code.path=builtin/normalize-keys.
- Emit metric sample of tokenizer token counts for each request (to see distribution drift).

Automated rollback rules (in Console/Ingress):
- If any abort threshold met for 2 consecutive evaluation windows (5m each) -> auto route switch to baseline. Send Slack alert to #serving-runtime and DM me + Jordan.
- Keep small window of suppressed alerts during initial ramp (so we don't spam).

Post-canary checks (if passed):
- Run longer 24h baseline vs canary A/B. Compute cost delta per million tokens (cpu/gpu time + egress).
- Run evaluation prompt set (15 prompts) to check semantic/regression (sampling deterministic seeds).
- Create follow-up tickets for cleanups: remove debug counters, tighten tests, consolidate metrics.

Open questions / gotchas:
- How does KV cache key normalization affect cross-request cache index? If we change key shape, warm misses will spike. Consider warming or dual-writing for short window.
- Is there any path that does heavy string allocations per request? Watch GC and heap growth.
- If we rely on header X-Canary, some clients (internal) might strip or not forward it. Consider route param as backup.
- Are we instrumenting the fallback path enough to confirm zero requests slip through old handler? (need unique trace ids).

Mini plan for dual-write (if we need warm cache migration):
- In canary code, when enabled, write both normalized_key and legacy_key to cache (ttl short). This doubles write but avoids cold misses during ramp.
- Monitor write amplification metrics; schedule expiry after 1 hour.

Quick PR checklist for reviewers (to paste into PR description):
- Summary: single-line explanation of what changes and why.
- Feature gate: flag name + default value.
- Observability: metrics added + tracing tags listed.
- Rollout plan: % ramp, time windows, abort thresholds.
- Backwards compat: dual-write strategy listed if applicable.
- Smoke test commands + expected outputs (examples).
- Manual rollback steps spelled out (exact Console clicks or CLI commands).

Notes to self (things to do while the PR is open):
- Add a small unit test for key normalization edgecases (unicode combining characters).
- Ask SRE to add alert channel for canary aborts (throttle controlled).
- Run local mem profiler with a synthetic 5k concurrent request spike to confirm heap behavior.
- Pair with Priya for the first production flip.

Meeting prep bullets (for 15-min sync):
- Brief: what the change is and why (1 slide).
- Risk summary: potential cache-warm miss, mem delta.
- Rollout timeline suggestion + who is on-call.
- Action: decide whether to dual-write or warm caches prior to flip.

Trash notes / iteration history:
- 2024-02-14 initial scratchpad
- 2024-02-20 added dual-write idea after spike in staging
- 2024-02-27 tightened thresholds after running small loadbench

If this works well, we should distill into a tiny canary checklist doc under shared_drives/product or eng-sre playbooks. For now: rough, actionable, and probably messy.

-- Selene
